title: Building an MMORPG with 100% LLM-driven (still very experimental pipeline)
author: Gaebabi
selftext:
I’m experimenting with making an MMORPG without manually editing code, Unity scenes, terrain, or data.

I only describe the desired result and review it. The LLM handles coding, terrain generation, villages, roads, NPCs, builds, testing, and screenshots using existing assets.

It already produces streamed terrain and playable Windows builds, but issues like broken rivers, misplaced buildings, and unnatural roads show the difference between “technically working” and “feeling like an MMORPG.”

Would you trust an LLM to manage an entire game-development pipeline?

comments.author: DoBRenkiY
comments.body: what's stack for client and server?

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body: I mainly used NestJS for the backend. For less critical but latency-sensitive real-time communication, I used Java with sockets.

comments.author: MindlessAd4611
comments.body:
Looks cool! Curious to see how far you will take it.

Trust in which way?  
There is no business critical operation happening behind the scenes, so if you play and it works, then it works no? I think that’s kind of the magic of LLM driven dev for non business applications.. you skip the massive bottleneck of reviewal, which enables absurdly fast iteration. 

I’m doing the same experiment with typescript and threejs, for a 2D maplestory style game.   
Having my mind blown each day by how fast and efficiently it progresses  🤯

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body: Your project sounds interesting too. I’m planning to post more updates as I go. thanks for checking it out!

comments.author: Exp5000
comments.body: I just really enjoy seeing what you guys come up with. Nice work dude

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body: Thanks! I’m still experimenting, but it’s been fun seeing how far the pipeline can go.

comments.author: niftler
comments.body: How much does all this cost to build?

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body: Codex shows roughly 2 billion tokens used, mostly while building and iterating on this map pipeline. I mainly used GPT-5.6 Terra on High reasoning.

comments.author: Emotional-Cat420
comments.body:
I'm all for Claude Code/Codex but I feel it can't solve creating high quality assets.

For example, what if you wish to create an attractive female model but also support armor layering with different armor items for head, body legs and arms...

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body: I agree. high-quality custom assets are still the biggest limitation. For this project, I’m using existing assets, and the LLM mainly handles selecting, configuring, and integrating them.

comments.author: Fulgren09
comments.body:
Your treatment of foliage and trees is really nice. You seem like a touch grass kind of person lol

Can I suggest 'dumb' shadows for the trees and placed until you figure something out better. 

Just want to point out that you are not merely building a game with an LLM pipeline, you are building an LLM pipeline that handles assets, rules, business logic, the game is just the output.

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body:
Yes, your last point is probably a more accurate description of the project. The game is basically the output of the pipeline.

I’m wondering what would happen if I added NPCs, stories, monsters, and bosses to the same pipeline. Maybe the LLM could connect them into a reasonably coherent world and generate a huge amount of content around them.

And if the NPCs themselves were also given some intelligence through an LLM... that could get really interesting.

replies.author: Fulgren09
replies.body:
You are on the right track with that line - its all about overlapping systems. LLM reads words, systems are in words (or math), so frontier agent with big context can keep all this in mind and assist you in building.

One thing that helped me are 'step back and consolidate' runs to help 'many things become one thing'.

comments.author: Successful_Cap_2177
comments.body: How is the token usage? Which LLM are you using and how do you orchestrate the pipeline for agents and prompt generation?

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body:
Codex reports roughly 2 billion tokens used while building and iterating on this map pipeline, including failed attempts. I mainly used GPT-5.6 Terra on High reasoning.

There wasn’t much special prompt engineering. the main thing I asked it to do was build the pipeline with an HTML viewer so I could watch its progress and outputs in real time.

That helped a lot because the AI and I could look at the same result, discuss what was wrong, and iterate from there. the viewer also gave me a practical way to limit its actions instead of letting it make changes blindly.

The orchestration itself is still fairly simple. one main agent edits the Unity project, runs tests and builds, captures the results, reviews them, and repeats. I’m not using a complex multi-agent framework yet.

replies.author: Successful_Cap_2177
replies.body:
With my pocs I found out that is really useful if you do a step zero for creating the roadmap and architecture with a high effort agent and from there onward I do with less capable agents specialized on gameplay dev, expansion dev(expand content where architecture is already defined) and testing agents.

With the roadmap it creates a nice feature map for allowing agents to act upon parallelization

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body: That sounds like a good structure. Right now I’m probably letting one agent handle too much, I’ll probably try separating architecture, implementation, content expansion, and testing next.

comments.author: bingewavecinema
comments.body:
Look good thus far. The hard part with LLMs isn't the developing and running locally, is how to maintain that state in real time for multiple users.

How are you incorpating that shared state?

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body: Do you mean the runtime state shared between in-game players, or the project state shared across AI agents or human developers?

replies.author: bingewavecinema
replies.body: Yes, run time shared between players

replies.author: Gaebabi
replies.body:
As shown in the video, the world is already divided into tiles. I plan to use those tiles as spatial partitions and assign each partition to a separate Java socket worker pool. 😄 

players would mainly receive updates from their current tile and nearby tiles, while the server remains authoritative. persistent state is handled separately through NestJS and TypeORM
